  func Popcount(xs []uint64) int {
  	n := 0
  	// Index-based main loop: one induction variable instead of reslicing
  	// xs every iteration. The 16-word window is a single reslice, so the

  	i := 0

diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
The cost has stayed at 3836 across three attempts with different loop shapes, so the current structure is probably near what SSA can do without a different algorithm. The main per-iteration overhead I can still trim is the reslice `xs = xs[16:]` and the loop-variable update. An index-based loop moves that work to a single integer `i`, and the tail is unchanged because `xs` is resliced to `xs[i:]` once after the loop.

This is a targeted change to the main loop only. The expected gain is modest, and I can't verify it without running giri.

Reasoning: the loop body performs 16 popcounts and adds per iteration, so the per-iteration overhead of reslicing (pointer, length, and capacity updates) is a real but small fraction of the cost. Moving to an integer index removes that bookkeeping from the hot path. The tail logic is untouched, and `xs` is still left unchanged since only the local slice header is reassigned. If this does not move the cost, the next lever is to unroll the main loop to 32 words to further amortize the loop back-edge, at the cost of code size.
